# Setting Up {#sec-setup .unnumbered}

## Registering for Earth Engine

**Who can use it free.** Earth Engine is free for **non-commercial** use: students, teachers, academic researchers, non-profit organisations and government work that is not sold. Everything in this book qualifies when you use it to learn, teach or do research. Work done for a paying client, or inside a company's product, is commercial and needs a paid Earth Engine subscription. Google may ask you to confirm that your use is non-commercial and applies usage limits to non-commercial projects; the book's scripts stay well inside them.

**Access now runs through a Google Cloud project.** You do not need a credit card for non-commercial use, but you do need a project to attach Earth Engine to:

1. Sign in with a Google account (a personal one is fine; a university account works too if your institution allows Google Cloud).
2. Open [console.cloud.google.com](https://console.cloud.google.com), create a project and note its **project ID** (for example `ee-yourname`).
3. Register that project for Earth Engine at [code.earthengine.google.com/register](https://code.earthengine.google.com/register): choose **unpaid usage**, then the non-commercial category that fits you (for example academia or research, or education), and answer the short questions about what you will do.
4. Open [code.earthengine.google.com](https://code.earthengine.google.com) and select the project if asked. If the map loads, you are ready.
5. For Python and Colab, authenticate once and name the same project: `ee.Authenticate()`, then `ee.Initialize(project="ee-yourname")`.

Approval is usually immediate or the same day. There is nothing to configure on your own machine.

::: {.callout-tip}
## If setting up a cloud project is a hurdle
Some readers cannot create a Google Cloud project, for example on a managed university or office account. You can still follow most of this book: **IJB**, the web-based Earth Engine app described in P10, runs in an ordinary browser with no account, no project and no code, and does a good job of the everyday analyses (composites, land cover, floods, fire, change). Open it at <https://rifkynauvalhsp.users.earthengine.app/view/ijbexplorer>.
:::

## Making scripts survive

Three habits keep work recoverable.

**Use repositories, not the untitled buffer.** Create a repository in the Scripts panel and save into it. Repositories are Git backed, so every save is versioned and any version is recoverable.

**Share by link, not by paste.** The **Get Link** button produces a URL carrying the script and its imports. A pasted script loses the Imports block, and the recipient gets an undefined variable error before reaching anything interesting.

**Name assets so they survive eighteen months.** `mangrove_training_mahakam_2023_v2` will still make sense. `training2` will not.

## The Python alternative

Everything in this book has a Python equivalent through the `earthengine-api` package, usually with `var` replaced by an assignment and camelCase method names unchanged.

```bash
pip install earthengine-api geemap
earthengine authenticate
```

```python
import ee, geemap
ee.Initialize(project="your-cloud-project")

aoi = ee.Geometry.Point([117.58, -0.84])
s2 = (ee.ImageCollection("COPERNICUS/S2_SR_HARMONIZED")
        .filterDate("2023-01-01", "2023-12-31")
        .filterBounds(aoi))

m = geemap.Map()
m.center_object(aoi, 10)
m.add_layer(s2.median(), {"bands": ["B4", "B3", "B2"], "min": 0, "max": 3000}, "Composite")
m
```

Choose Python when Earth Engine is one stage of a longer pipeline, when you need libraries the platform does not offer, or when results must be reproducible outside a browser. Choose JavaScript when you want the Inspector, instant sharing and no environment to maintain.

## Building this book locally

The project renders with [Quarto](https://quarto.org). No R or Python knowledge is needed beyond having Python 3 available for the snippet generator.

```bash
quarto preview                 # live reloading local site
quarto render --to html        # static site in _book/
quarto render --to pdf         # requires a LaTeX install
quarto install tinytex         # the easiest way to get one
```

The `pre-render` step regenerates `_snippets/` from `scripts/`, so edit the `.js` files and never the snippets.
